extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students in combinatorial geometry / discrete mathematics interested in Borsuk's conjecture and the Kahn–Kalai construction
extracted.subtask_description: Verify and/or reproduce the Kahn–Kalai construction of point sets that (may) disprove Borsuk's conjecture: choose k (prime power), set m=4k, build the 0–1 vector point set K, compute the combinatorial lower bound q on the number of subsets of smaller diameter and compare q to the embedding dimension d to decide if K is a counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borsuk's conjecture (formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether each bounded set in the n-dimensional Euclidean space can be divided into n+1 parts of smaller diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A counterexample is a bounded set in R^n that cannot be partitioned into n+1 parts each having strictly smaller diameter than the whole set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larman's finite-sets translation (special (0,1)-vectors case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K be a family of k-subsets of {1,2,...,n} such that every two members of K have t elements in common. Then K can be partitioned into n parts so that in each part every two members have (t+1) elements in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disproving this finite-set statement for the translated parameters implies a disproof of Borsuk's conjecture for the corresponding geometric construction of 0–1 vectors with constant weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frankl–Wilson theorem (instantiated bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let k be a prime power and n = 4k. Let K be a family of n/2-subsets of {1,2,...,n} so that no two sets in the family have intersection of size n/4. Then |K| ≤ binomial(n−1, n/4−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combinatorial upper bound on the size of families with restricted intersections is the key tool to bound the size of subsets of the constructed point set that have smaller diameter (i.e., to bound how many points can appear in any single piece of a partition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction parameters (m and V) and nature of K
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose k a prime power and set m = 4k; let V = {1,2,...,m}. The construction produces a point set K of 0–1-vectors (index set W of size 2k) lying in a hyperplane; the point set K lies in Euclidean space of dimension d strictly less than m/2 − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the formal construction: consider certain 2k-subsets A ⊂ V, form corresponding 0–1 vectors S(A) (and complementary relations N(A)), and take K = {S(A)}. Treat K as 0–1-vectors with constant weight so that all vectors lie in the same hyperplane; compute the embedding dimension d from the construction (d is the dimension of the affine span).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiation bound for subsets of smaller diameter (R(T) bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: For T ⊂ K with diam(T) < M (M the diameter of K), the instantiated Frankl–Wilson bound gives |R(T)| ≤ binomial(m−1, k−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this bound on |R(T)| (the related combinatorial object associated to T) to count how many points can lie in any single part of a partition of K into sets of smaller diameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound q on the number of parts needed (combinatorial q)
rubrics_metrics.description: The point set K cannot be covered by q subsets of smaller diameter; q is given by a combinatorial expression (as derived) and the paper provides equivalent forms, e.g. q = 2 * (3k choose k)/(2k choose k) (alternative equivalent expressions are shown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute q using the provided combinatorial formulae (the paper gives two convenient product/summation forms that require only a few multiplications and one division). The paper emphasizes that its corrected derivation yields values of q double those given in the original Kahn–Kalai sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for K to be a counterexample (q versus d)
rubrics_metrics.description: If q > d + 1 then K is a counterexample to Borsuk's conjecture in dimension d and in every higher dimension below q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After computing d (dimension of the affine span of K) and q (minimal number of smaller-diameter parts needed to cover K), verify the inequality q > d+1 to conclude the constructed K is a counterexample. This is the decisive numeric test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct counting / doubling correction
rubrics_metrics.description: The original derivation in [3] omitted the fact that each of the partitions used to construct K exclusively contains two subsets of V, which caused the resulting upper bound to be exactly double of what a careful count gives; correcting this removes one final halving and doubles the lower bound q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reproducing the combinatorial count, ensure that partitions/pairings of subsets of V are accounted for correctly (do not introduce an unjustified halving). The corrected formula produces q values twice as large as the original sketch in [3], expanding the range of dimensions verified as counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal distance implies intersection size k
rubrics_metrics.description: In the construction, dist(S(A), S(B)) is maximal (equals the diameter M) if and only if |A ∩ B| = k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To identify which pairs of 0–1 vectors realize the diameter of K, verify that their corresponding underlying 2k-subsets intersect in exactly k elements; this fact is used in the derivation of which subsets T have diam(T) = M and which have diam(T) < M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical numeric verification for k values
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute d and q for specific k (prime power) values and check q > d+1; the paper lists computed results (e.g., k=13 gives d=1325 and a q value large enough so that K is a counterexample for 1325; similar listings for k=16,17,29,31,32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the explicit combinatorial formulas (or the few-multiplications forms the paper provides) to compute q numerically for candidate k values. The paper provides sample numeric outputs and flags which k produce verified counterexamples under the corrected formula.
